message.content:
Below is a concise overview of the key rights and protections you have as a tenant in Texas. (This is general information and not legal advice; for specific situations you may want to consult an attorney or a local tenant‑rights organization.) | Area | What the law says | Practical Tips | |------|-------------------|----------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to one month’s rent for a furnished unit, two months for an unfurnished unit.
• Must be returned within 30 days after you move out, minus any lawful deductions.
• Landlord must provide a written itemized list of deductions. | • Keep a copy of the lease and any receipts for repairs you made.
• Inspect the unit before moving out and document any existing damage. | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must keep the premises in a safe, sanitary condition (e.g., plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity).
• Must comply with all building, housing, and health codes. | • Report problems in writing (email or letter) and keep copies.
• If the landlord fails to fix major issues, you may withhold rent or repair and deduct, but do so only after following the proper notice procedures. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease.
• Late fees are allowed only if the lease states them and they are reasonable. | • Pay on time or negotiate a payment plan if you’re having trouble. | | **Notice to Vacate** | • For month‑to‑month leases, either party must give at least 30 days’ written notice.
• For fixed‑term leases, the lease ends automatically unless you break it (see below). | • Provide written notice (email or letter) and keep a copy. | | **Breaking a Lease** | • You can terminate a lease early if the landlord breaches the lease (e.g., fails to maintain habitability).
• You may also break a lease for “just cause” (e.g., domestic violence, job relocation) under certain circumstances. | • Document the landlord’s breach and give written notice.
• Keep records of any communication. | | **Privacy & Entry** | • Landlord must give at least 24 hours’ written notice before entering, except in emergencies.
• Entry is allowed for repairs, inspections, or showing the unit to prospective tenants. | • Ask for a written notice of entry and keep a log of visits. | | **Discrimination** | • Texas law (and federal Fair Housing Act) prohibits discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or other protected classes. | • If you suspect discrimination, file a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for non‑payment, 30‑day notice for lease termination).
• If you fail to comply, the landlord can file an unlawful detainer action.
• You have the right to contest the eviction in court. | • Respond promptly to notices.
• Keep copies of all notices and communications. | | **Repair & Deduct** | • If the landlord fails to fix a major problem, you may repair it yourself and deduct the cost from your rent, but you must follow the proper notice and documentation steps. | • Get written permission first; if denied, you may still proceed but must keep detailed records. | | **Rent Control** | • Texas does not have statewide rent control; rent increases are governed by the lease terms. | • Review your lease for any rent‑increase clauses. | | **Utilities** | • The lease should specify who pays utilities. | • Verify utility responsibilities before signing. | | **Subletting & Assignment** | • Many leases allow subletting or assignment with landlord’s consent. | • Obtain written consent and keep a copy. | | **Landlord’s Right to Inspect** | • Landlord may inspect the unit for maintenance or to show it to prospective tenants, but must give notice. | • Keep a log of inspections. | | **Legal Resources** | • Texas Attorney General’s Office, Texas Commission on Human Rights, local tenant‑rights groups, and legal aid clinics. | • Contact them for help if you face eviction or discrimination. | ### Quick Checklist Before Signing a Lease 1. **Read the lease thoroughly** – look for clauses on rent, security deposit, maintenance responsibilities, notice periods, and any penalties. 2. **Ask about habitability** – confirm that the landlord will maintain plumbing, heating, electrical, and structural safety. 3. **Verify the security deposit limit** – ensure it does not exceed the statutory maximum. 4. **Check for “no‑late‑fee” clauses** – if the lease allows late fees, confirm they are reasonable. 5. **Confirm who pays utilities** – make sure it’s clearly stated. 6. **Ask about subletting** – if you might need to sublet, get written permission. --- #### When Things Go Wrong - **Landlord fails to maintain habitability**: Notify in writing, give a reasonable deadline, and keep copies. If the landlord still doesn’t fix it, you may withhold rent or repair and deduct, but follow the proper procedure. - **Unlawful eviction notice**: Respond in writing, keep copies, and consider filing a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights if you suspect discrimination. - **Discrimination**: File a complaint with the Texas Commission on Human Rights or HUD. --- #### Useful Contacts | Resource | Contact | |----------|---------| | Texas Attorney General – Consumer Protection | https://www.texasattorneygeneral.gov/consumer-protection | | Texas Commission on Human Rights | https://www.tchra.org/ | | HUD – Fair Housing | https://www.hud.gov/ | | Local Legal Aid (e.g., Texas Legal Services Center) | https://www.texaslegalservices.org/ | | Tenant‑Rights Organizations (e.g., Texas Tenants Union) | https://www.texastenantsunion.org/ | Feel free to ask if you need more detail on any specific point or if you’d like help drafting a notice or a repair‑and‑deduct letter.
